_meta.source: JUNIT (JUnit Tutorial, JUnit 4, 8 p.), MOCK (SmartBear, 12 p.), TDM (DZone Refcard, 9 p.), JMETER (JMeter Tutorial 2.11, 53 p.), SWE-G (ch. 11-14, PDF p.149-221)
_meta.page_convention: PDF pages; printed JMETER = N-7; MOCK and TDM PDF = printed; SWE-G has no printed numbering
_meta.note: rules = stated in the source with a page; not_in_book = NOT in the source (label [extrapolation]); uncovered = topics with no coverage. Keywords keep the Portuguese input terms and add English ones.

piramide-80-15-5.name: Test pyramid: 80/15/5
piramide-80-15-5.summary: Google speaks of roughly 80% unit tests, 15% integration and 5% end-to-end, by test case count; each team varies.
rules: Approximate 80/15/5 mix by count of test cases (SWE-G p.156)
In ch. 12: about 80% unit tests and 20% of broader scope (SWE-G p.165)
Anti-patterns ice cream cone and hourglass (SWE-G p.156-157)
The mix should reflect the local architectural and organizational reality (SWE-G p.157)
not_in_book: 70/20/10 is NOT in the SWE-G testing chapters (the book says 80/15/5)

tamanho-escopo.name: Test size and scope (small, medium, large)
tamanho-escopo.summary: Size = the test's resources; scope = the code verified. Small: one process, no sleep/I/O/network; medium: one machine (localhost); large: no restriction.
rules: Size and scope are distinct dimensions (SWE-G p.153)
Small: one process; no sleep, I/O or blocking calls; uses test doubles (SWE-G p.154)
Medium: several processes and threads, network only to localhost (SWE-G p.154)
Large: may span several machines; reserved for configuration E2E and legacy without doubles (SWE-G p.155)
In practice Google has a fourth size, enormous (SWE-G p.163, note 4)
Narrow scope (unit), medium (integration), broad (E2E/system) (SWE-G p.156)

flaky-hermetico.name: Flaky tests and hermetic tests
flaky-hermetico.summary: Flaky = non-deterministic failure. The book quantifies the cost (0.1% x 10,000 tests = 10 flakes/day), says that near 1% tests lose value and asks for hermetic tests.
rules: Sources of non-determinism: clock, threads, network latency (SWE-G p.155)
Example: 0.1% spurious failure and 10,000 tests/day = 10 investigations per day; near 1% value is lost; Google's rate ~0.15% (SWE-G p.155)
Automatically re-running trades CPU for engineering time and only postpones the root cause (SWE-G p.155)
A hermetic test contains everything it needs to set up, run and tear down the environment, without depending on order or a shared database (SWE-G p.155)
sleep/setTimeout are naive heuristics; poll the state with a timeout (SWE-G p.159, p.219)
Fixing broken tests within minutes keeps confidence (SWE-G p.152)
not_in_book: Immediately quarantining flaky tests is not a prescription of the book [inference]

beyonce-falhas-cobertura.name: Beyoncé Rule, failure testing and coverage
beyonce-falhas-cobertura.summary: Test everything you do not want to break; simulate failures; coverage measures execution, not verification, and targets become ceilings.
rules: Beyoncé Rule: if you care about it, put a test on it (SWE-G p.157)
Test failures: exceptions in unit tests, RPC errors/latency in integration and E2E (SWE-G p.157)
Coverage measures invoked lines; an 80% target becomes a ceiling; measure only small tests (SWE-G p.157-158)

testes-unitarios-claros.name: Clear and stable unit tests
testes-unitarios-claros.summary: Tests that do not change on refactoring, use the public API, verify state, are complete and concise, test behaviors and prefer DAMP over DRY.
rules: Strive for unchanging tests: only a change in behavior requires changing the test (SWE-G p.166-167)
Test through the public API, not the private ones (SWE-G p.167-169)
State, not interaction (SWE-G p.169-170)
Complete and concise (SWE-G p.171-172); behaviors, not methods (SWE-G p.172-173)
Given/when/then, also called arrange/act/assert (SWE-G p.173; p.183 note 6)
The name describes the action and result; starting with 'should' is a trick (SWE-G p.174-175)
No logic in the test (SWE-G p.175-176); clear failure messages (SWE-G p.176-177)
DAMP, not DRY (SWE-G p.177-179)
Shared values via helpers/builders; setup only to construct the object under test (SWE-G p.179-181)
Shared test infrastructure has its own tests (SWE-G p.182)

test-doubles.name: Test doubles: vocabulary and stance
test-doubles.summary: SWE-G organizes three techniques (faking, stubbing, interaction testing) and prefers the real implementation; MOCK uses stub/mock/virtual service.
rules: A test double replaces a real implementation; the chapter avoids 'mocking' as a synonym (SWE-G p.184)
Concerns: testability, applicability, fidelity (SWE-G p.184-185)
Abuse of mocking frameworks at Google: tests costly to maintain that rarely found bugs (SWE-G p.185)
Seams and dependency injection (SWE-G p.186-187)
Three techniques: faking, stubbing, interaction testing (SWE-G p.188-189)
First choice: the real implementation; classical vs mockist style (SWE-G p.189-190)
@DoNotMock (SWE-G p.190-191)
MOCK: stub, mock and virtual service (MOCK p.4)
not_in_book: Dummy and Spy do NOT appear in SWE-G or MOCK; the Meszaros taxonomy is an [extrapolation]

fakes.name: Fakes
fakes.summary: A fake = a lightweight implementation faithful to the contract; it should be written and maintained by the API owner and have its own tests.
rules: A fake is a lightweight implementation of the API, unsuitable for production (SWE-G p.188)
The team that owns the real implementation writes and maintains the fake; create it at the root of what is not fit for tests (SWE-G p.193)
Fidelity to the API contract; fail fast on unsupported paths (SWE-G p.194)
Fakes should have tests, run against both the real one and the fake (SWE-G p.194)
No fake: ask the owners; or wrap the API in a class and fake that (SWE-G p.194-195)

stubbing-interacao.name: Stubbing and interaction testing
stubbing-interacao.summary: Excess stubbing and interaction testing produce brittle tests; prefer state testing; interaction only in specific cases.
rules: Dangers of stubbing: unclear, brittle and less effective tests (SWE-G p.195-196)
Stubbing is appropriate to drive the system into a state or simulate errors; stub few functions (SWE-G p.197)
Prefer state testing; interaction testing does not prove correctness; nicknamed change-detector tests (SWE-G p.197-198)
Legitimate interaction testing: no real one or fake, or when the number/order of calls matters (SWE-G p.198)
Only for state-changing functions (e.g. sendEmail), and without over-specifying (SWE-G p.198-200)

junit4-anotacoes.name: JUnit 4: annotations and lifecycle
rules: @Test marks a public void method as a test (JUNIT p.3)
@Before/@After per test; @BeforeClass/@AfterClass once and static (JUNIT p.3)
Order shown by the example (JUNIT p.3)
@Ignore on a method or class (JUNIT p.3, p.6)
not_in_book: JUnit 5 (@BeforeEach, @DisplayName, @Nested, assertAll) is NOT in the PDF

junit4-asserts.name: JUnit 4: assertions
junit4-asserts.summary: org.junit.Assert: assertEquals, assertTrue, assertFalse, assertNull, assertNotNull, assertSame, assertNotSame, assertArrayEquals.
rules: Table of assertions with an optional message (JUNIT p.3-4)
A failure aborts the test and appears in the JUnit window (JUNIT p.4)
not_in_book: assertThrows, assertAll, assertTimeout are NOT in the PDF

junit4-suites-param-rules.name: JUnit 4: suites, parameterized tests, Rules, Categories, CLI
junit4-suites-param-rules.summary: Suites with @RunWith/@Suite, parameterized tests with @Parameters, @Rule, @Category and execution through JUnitCore.
rules: @RunWith(Suite.class) with @Suite.SuiteClasses (JUNIT p.7)
Parameterized: constructor, static @Parameters method and @Test (JUNIT p.7)
@Rule: ErrorCollector, ExpectedException, TestName (JUNIT p.7)
@Category, @IncludeCategory, @ExcludeCategory (JUNIT p.7-8)
JUnitCore.runClasses and Result/Failure; junit-4.11.jar and hamcrest-core-1.3.jar (JUNIT p.8)

api-mocking-vocab.name: API mocking: stub, mock, virtual service
api-mocking-vocab.summary: The SmartBear e-book defines stub, mock and virtual service and says when to use each.
rules: Stub: minimal version with predictable data, often handwritten (MOCK p.4)
Mock: verifies outputs against expectations, focuses on interactions, usually has state (MOCK p.4)
Virtual service: created from a definition (OAS) or from recorded traffic; remote and shared (MOCK p.4)
Virtual services in system tests; stubs and mocks in unit/module/acceptance tests (MOCK p.4)
not_in_book: 'Static vs dynamic' mocks and in-memory CRUD are NOT in MOCK

contract-testing.name: Contract testing
contract-testing.summary: Contract testing verifies each application in isolation against a shared contract; SWE-G cites Pact and Spring Cloud Contracts.
rules: Contract testing: each application in isolation against a contract of the messages (MOCK p.5)
Applies where two services communicate; pays off with many microservices (MOCK p.5)
Helps control mock drift (MOCK p.7)
Consumer-driven: Pact and Spring Cloud Contracts; Google does not use them because of protocol buffers (SWE-G p.210)
In SWE-G, contract tests are also the tests run against the real one and the fake (SWE-G p.194)
not_in_book: Pact broker, can-i-deploy and contract versioning are NOT in the sources

mock-drift-quando-mockar.name: When to mock and mock drift
mock-drift-quando-mockar.summary: Mock when the service does not exist or the dependency is unavailable; mocks diverge from the real one (drift).
rules: Recommendation: service not yet developed or dependencies unavailable (MOCK p.6)
Mock drift and contract testing (MOCK p.7)
Problems of the real service in tests: connectivity, slowness, rate limits, lack of a sandbox (MOCK p.9)
Use cases: API design, collaboration, demonstration (MOCK p.8)
SWE-G: do not use a real third-party API in automated tests (SWE-G p.209)
not_in_book: Simulating HTTP 500/503/429 is NOT described in MOCK

gravacao-replay.name: Traffic recording and replay
gravacao-replay.summary: Record the traffic of an API and replay it in tests (MOCK) and Google's Record/Replay model (SWE-G).
rules: MOCK: record HTTP/HTTPS traffic and create a virtual service; forward to the real API (MOCK p.9-10)
SWE-G: a larger test in Record Mode generates logs; Replay Mode in development; matchers (SWE-G p.210)

tdm-visao.name: TDM: overview and data factory
tdm-visao.summary: Refcard with patterns and anti-patterns per TDM method; data requirements should be captured early.
rules: TDM builds data-ready environments across the SDLC (TDM p.1)
Natural complexity of data (TDM p.1)
Data factory: requirements, profiling, synthetic data, subsetting, virtualization, masking/encryption, validation, orchestration, views, exemptions (TDM p.3)
Data requirements per user story; anti-pattern: capturing them late (TDM p.3-4)

tdm-profiling-sinteticos.name: TDM: profiling and synthetic data
tdm-profiling-sinteticos.summary: Automatic profiling finds PII; synthetic data avoids production in early phases but does not suit every phase.
rules: Automated profiling discovers schema, relationships and PII; anti-pattern: manual (TDM p.4)
Synthetic data: avoid production and create data that does not exist (TDM p.4)
Anti-pattern: using fake data in higher environments (SIT, UAT, performance) (TDM p.5)

tdm-masking-encryption.name: TDM: masking and encryption
tdm-masking-encryption.summary: Masking is non-reversible and should keep a production-like appearance; encryption is reversible by key. Anti-patterns: masking too much and masking inconsistently.
rules: Masking: a copy with obfuscated PII, preferably non-reversible (TDM p.6)
Benefits: aligns with GDPR, HIPAA and PCI (TDM p.6)
Anti-patterns: over-protecting; protecting inconsistently (TDM p.6)
Encryption: reversible with a key; DES, AES, RSA; loses the format (TDM p.6)
not_in_book: LGPD is NOT cited; SDM/DDM (static/dynamic masking) are NOT in TDM

tdm-validacao-views-orquestracao.name: TDM: validation, views and orchestration
tdm-validacao-views-orquestracao.summary: Automatically validate PII removal; views reserve data pools; automate the data operations.
rules: Validation: a screening process; anti-pattern: manual inspection (TDM p.6-7)
Data views and pool reservation; anti-pattern: list/spreadsheet (TDM p.7)
Orchestration: standardize and automate; anti-patterns: the hero and selective automation (TDM p.7)

tdm-subsetting-virtualizacao.name: TDM: subsetting and virtualization
tdm-subsetting-virtualizacao.summary: Subsetting reduces the footprint by a repeatable criterion and must be precise; virtualization uses deltas over the source.
rules: Subsetting by a repeatable criterion; benefits: lower cost and less batch time (TDM p.5)
Anti-pattern: a loose subset loses data and relationships (TDM p.5)
Virtualization: deltas between the source and the local copy (TDM p.5)
Anti-patterns: data not desensitized in the source; transforming the delta (TDM p.5)
not_in_book: Copy-on-Write, sampling percentages and restore times are NOT in TDM

tdm-exemptions-reporting.name: TDM: exemptions and reporting
tdm-exemptions-reporting.summary: Production data only as a last resort, with a request and a recorded window; DataOps and DataSec reporting.
rules: Exemptions: last resort; request, documented risk, approval and window (TDM p.8)
Anti-pattern: exemption as standard practice (TDM p.8)
DataOps and DataSec reporting; anti-patterns: not reporting and reporting manually (TDM p.8)

jmeter-thread-group.name: JMeter: Thread Group
jmeter-thread-group.summary: The Thread Group is the root of the plan: threads, ramp-up, loop count, error behavior and scheduler.
rules: Root of the plan (JMETER p.15)
Number of threads, ramp-up period, loop count, error behavior (JMETER p.15)
Scheduler: start and end (JMETER p.15)
Recording example: 50 threads, ramp-up 10 s, 1 loop (JMETER p.42)
not_in_book: Thread calculation (Little's Law) is NOT in JMETER

jmeter-componentes-ordem.name: JMeter: components and order of execution
jmeter-componentes-ordem.summary: Test plan with samplers, controllers, listeners, timers, config elements, pre/post processors; the order of execution is on p.21.
rules: Samplers (JMETER p.15-16); logic controllers (JMETER p.16-17); listeners (JMETER p.17)
Timers; without a timer, the next request goes out immediately (JMETER p.18)
Config elements, pre processors (JMETER p.19); post processors (JMETER p.20)
Order: config, pre, timers, sampler, post, assertions, listeners (JMETER p.21)

jmeter-assertions.name: JMeter: assertions and extractors
jmeter-assertions.summary: Assertions validate the response; examples with Duration (100 ms, 2000 ms) and Size (5000 bytes); regex/XPath/CSS extractors.
rules: List of assertions (JMETER p.18)
A 100 ms Duration Assertion fails; with 2000 ms almost everything passes (JMETER p.29-30)
5000-byte Size Assertion (JMETER p.30-31)
Post processors: Regular Expression, XPath, CSS/JQuery Extractor (JMETER p.20)
not_in_book: JSON Path Extractor is NOT in the 2.11 list; Response Assertion is not described in detail

jmeter-nongui-boaspraticas.name: JMeter: non-GUI and best practices
jmeter-nongui-boaspraticas.summary: Experienced users run in non-GUI: jmeter -n -t plano.jmx -l resultado.jtl; few listeners; Stop and Shutdown.
rules: Non-GUI: jmeter -n -t test.jmx -l test.jtl (JMETER p.50)
Listeners consume a lot of memory; use few (JMETER p.50)
View only errors; variables and loops instead of duplicated samplers; meaningful messages (JMETER p.50)
Stop (Ctrl+.) and Shutdown (Ctrl+,) (JMETER p.50)
Jenkins Performance plugin (JMETER p.49)
not_in_book: -e -o (HTML dashboard) is NOT in the PDF: [extrapolation], versions later than 2.11

jmeter-planos-exemplo.name: JMeter: example plans (HTTP, JDBC, JUnit, recording)
jmeter-planos-exemplo.summary: The tutorial builds HTTP, JDBC (MySQL), JUnit plans and a recording through a proxy.
rules: HTTP plan with a 500 ms timer and assertions (JMETER p.25-31)
JDBC plan with MySQL (JMETER p.32-36)
Plan with JUnit Request; jar in lib/junit (JMETER p.37-40)
Recording with a Firefox proxy and the Test Script Recorder (JMETER p.41-48)

testes-grandes.name: Larger tests (SWE-G ch. 14)
testes-grandes.summary: Larger tests exist to cover fidelity; they have costs (slow, flaky, owners, standardization).
rules: Fidelity is the primary reason for larger tests (SWE-G p.202-203)
Gaps of unit tests: unfaithful doubles, configuration, load, unanticipated behaviors, emergent behaviors (SWE-G p.203-204)
Challenges: reliability, speed, scale, ownership and standardization (SWE-G p.204-205)
Structure: obtain the SUT, seed data, act, verify (SWE-G p.207)
SUT: single process, single machine, multi-machine, shared environments, hybrids (SWE-G p.208)
Keep the SUT as small as possible; handle UI/API boundaries and third parties (SWE-G p.207, p.209)
Documented owners for larger tests (SWE-G p.220-221)

tipos-de-testes-grandes.name: Types of larger tests
tipos-de-testes-grandes.summary: Google's list: functional, browser/device, performance/load/stress, configuration, exploratory, A/B diff, UAT, probers and canary, DiRT/chaos, user evaluation.
rules: Types listed (SWE-G p.211-212)
Performance, load and stress: emergent properties; imitate production (SWE-G p.213)
Configuration test: smoke test of the SUT with its configuration files (SWE-G p.213)
Exploratory and bug bash (SWE-G p.213-214)
A/B diff and A-A (SWE-G p.214-215)
UAT (SWE-G p.215); probers and canary (SWE-G p.215-216)
DiRT and chaos engineering (SWE-G p.216-217)
Dogfooding, experimentation, evaluation by raters (SWE-G p.217)

dados-testes-grandes.name: Data in larger tests
dados-testes-grandes.summary: Seeded data and test traffic; sources: handcrafted, copied, sampled.
rules: Seeded data and test traffic (SWE-G p.210)
Handcrafted, copied and sampled data; smart sampling (SWE-G p.210-211)

uncovered.note: JUnit 5/Jupiter is NOT in the sources (JUNIT is a JUnit 4 tutorial). The JUnit 4 -> 5 map in references/ciclo-de-vida-e-assercoes-junit.md, section 5, is an [extrapolation].
The Meszaros taxonomy (Dummy, Stub, Spy, Mock, Fake) is NOT in SWE-G or MOCK: [extrapolation].
Little's Law, throughput and percentiles are NOT in JMETER: [extrapolation]; use jmeter_calc.py, which labels the calculations.
LGPD, static/dynamic masking and Copy-on-Write are NOT in TDM (which cites GDPR, HIPAA and PCI): [extrapolation].
Tools and techniques outside the sources (SWE-G uses Mockito in its examples and mentions Cucumber and WebDriver in passing): [extrapolation].
